Monet And The Seven Minute Light

art 17 Aug 2026

Sentence34 words · 0.2 min

One wall, about thirty canvases, each at its own hour.

Monet painted the same haystack, cathedral and pond for thirty years because his subject was never the thing — it was the light on it, and the light holds still for about seven minutes.

The stacks in the field at Giverny, where the method began.

In the summer of 1890, in a field near his house at Giverny, Monet noticed that the wheat stacks he had begun in the morning were wrong by lunchtime. Not badly drawn — simply no longer true, because the light had moved. His solution was to stop trying to finish. He set up several canvases at once, worked each for as long as its light lasted, and swapped when it changed. The result was the first great series: fifteen versions of the same stacks, sold out within days in 1891. Poplars, Rouen Cathedral, the Thames and his own water garden followed.

Impression, soleil levant, 1872. The painting that gave Impressionism its name — and its worst review.

Monet painted the same subject over and over because what he was after was the light on it, and light will not hold still. The name for that project came from a joke. In 1874 a group rejected by the official Salon mounted their own show in a photographer’s studio on the Boulevard des Capucines. Monet submitted a hazy view of Le Havre at dawn and, asked for a title, said it could hardly be called a view — call it an impression. The critic Louis Leroy seized on the word and mocked it. The insult stuck to the whole group, and they adopted it.

The technique behind the joke was serious. Monet painted outdoors, fast, in broken strokes of unmixed colour laid side by side so that they mix in the eye rather than on the palette. Shadows, in his work, are not black or brown; they are blue, violet, green — the complement of whatever light is falling nearby. It looks careless up close and resolves at a distance, which is precisely how vision works, and it was the only way to record something that would be gone in a few minutes.

The series paintings pushed this to its logical end. If light is the subject, then one canvas can only be a single sentence about it, and you need a paragraph. Between 1892 and 1894 he rented rooms opposite Rouen Cathedral and produced about thirty canvases of the same stone façade: grey and dissolved at dawn, gold at midday, burning at sunset. He is said to have wept over them, terrified of a change in the weather, and to have dreamed the cathedral was falling on him.

The problem he set himself

Painting outdoors was not new, but painting an unfinished, moving effect and calling it done was. Monet’s generation had access to two things their teachers did not: metal tubes of ready-mixed oil paint, which made a day in a field possible, and new synthetic pigments — cobalt violet, cerulean, chrome yellow — bright enough to stand in for sunlight. What they lacked was any tradition for the thing they wanted to record, which was not an object but a condition.

Working in parallel

The series method was practical before it was philosophical. Monet would arrive at a motif with a cart of canvases, sometimes a dozen or more, and cycle through them as the hour changed, returning day after day to the same canvas at the same hour. His stepdaughter Blanche carried the wheelbarrow. He would abandon a canvas the moment its light failed to return — and then, contradicting himself, take the whole set back to the studio and work them for months, tuning each against the others until the set held together as a set.

Wheatstacks, End of Summer, 1890–91. One of about twenty-five canvases of the same field.

Rouen, 1892–1894

The cathedral series is the extreme case: a flat wall of Gothic stone, chosen precisely because it offered nothing to look at except surface and shadow. The paint is built up so thickly in places that it becomes stone-like itself, a physical crust standing in for the carved one. Thirty canvases; twenty shown together in 1895. Clemenceau, then a newspaper editor and later Prime Minister, wrote that the series revealed a wall of stone as a thing in continuous change, and urged the state to buy the lot.

Giverny

From 1883 Monet rented a house in a village on the Seine, forty miles from Paris; in 1890, finally solvent, he bought it. He then did something no painter had done at that scale: he built his own subject. He diverted a stream, dug a pond, planted willows, bamboo and irises, imported water lilies, and had a Japanese-style footbridge built over the water. Gardeners were hired to keep the surface clear of dust. From about 1897 until his death in 1926 he painted almost nothing else — around 250 canvases of the same few square metres of water.

The late work

By 1912 cataracts had turned his sight yellow-brown, and he painted increasingly from memory of what colours should be, labelling his tubes and keeping them in strict order. He had the lens of his right eye removed in 1923; afterwards, with no lens to filter ultraviolet, he could see blues and violets most people cannot, and several late canvases show it. The last project, the Grandes Décorations, was a set of vast curved water-lily panels promised to France on the day after the 1918 armistice. He worked on them for eight years, refused to let them be shown, and they were installed at the Orangerie in Paris in 1927, a few months after he died.

A slow start

Oscar-Claude Monet was born in Paris in 1840 and grew up in Le Havre, where he made his first money drawing caricatures of local worthies for fifteen francs each. The painter Eugène Boudin, who worked on the beaches there, dragged him outdoors and taught him to paint from the motif rather than from the studio. Monet later said that the moment his eyes were opened, and he truly understood nature, was the day Boudin made him look at the sky over the Channel.

The next twenty years were hard in a way that the serene late paintings conceal entirely. He failed to gain a footing at the Salon, ran out of money repeatedly, moved to escape creditors, and in 1868 wrote to a friend that he had been thrown out of an inn, penniless, with his family. His companion and model Camille Doncieux bore their son Jean in 1867; they married in 1870. She died in 1879, aged thirty-two, and Monet painted her on her deathbed — then wrote, with real horror at himself, that he had caught himself analysing the arrangement of the colours death was laying on her face. That reflex, the eye running ahead of the man, is the whole story of his working life in one sentence.

Impression, and the insult that stuck

The first exhibition of the Société Anonyme des Artistes Peintres, Sculpteurs, Graveurs — thirty painters including Degas, Renoir, Pissarro, Cézanne and Berthe Morisot — opened in April 1874. Monet showed a small canvas of Le Havre harbour, orange sun over blue-grey mist, the water indicated with a few horizontal drags of paint. Impression, soleil levant.

Louis Leroy’s review in Le Charivari took the form of a comic dialogue with an imaginary academic painter who slowly goes mad in front of the pictures. “Impression — of course. There must be an impression in there somewhere,” he has the man say. The word was intended to convey that the work was a sketch pretending to be a painting. Within a few years the painters were using it themselves.

What the joke missed is that the painting is accurate. The sun in that canvas is almost exactly the same brightness as the sky around it — measured with modern instruments, its luminance barely differs from the background — which is why it seems to pulse. Monet had painted the way the eye actually receives a low sun through mist: colour separated from brightness. The academic tradition would have made the sun the brightest thing on the canvas because it is the brightest thing in the world. Monet painted what arrives at the retina.

The invention of the series

In 1890 he began the stacks. These were not the small hay bales of English fields but meules — grain stacks the height of a small house, standing in the field near his house through autumn and winter until threshing. They were, as subjects, almost aggressively boring: two shapes in a field. That was the point. With the subject held constant, everything that changed on the canvas had to be light.

He described the discipline in a letter: he was working with great difficulty, obstinately, on a series of different effects, but at this time of year the sun sets so fast that he could not keep up. Fifteen of the canvases went on show at Durand-Ruel’s gallery in May 1891, priced at three to four thousand francs each. They sold out in days. For the first time in his life, Monet was rich.

The method then repeated. Poplars along the river Epte in 1891 — when the trees were sold for timber halfway through, he bought them himself and paid the buyer to leave them standing until he had finished. Rouen Cathedral, 1892–94. Mornings on the Seine. The Thames from a window at the Savoy, and the Houses of Parliament in fog, painted over three winter visits between 1899 and 1901.

Rouen Cathedral, west façade in sunlight, 1894. About thirty canvases of the same stone wall at different hours.

The London series contains a detail that dates it precisely. The famous “London fog” Monet painted was not fog. It was smog — coal smoke from a million domestic grates and factory chimneys mixing with river mist — and it is why his Thames pictures are yellow, orange and violet rather than grey. He complained bitterly when a clear day arrived and ruined the effect.

Building the subject

The Giverny garden is Monet’s largest work, and the only one that needed six gardeners. He bought the property in 1890 and, two years later, a strip of marshy land across the road and the railway line, through which the little river Ru ran. He applied to the local council for permission to divert it into a pond, and the application caused a small scandal: neighbours worried that his strange foreign plants would poison the water their cattle drank.

He won, dug the pond, and built the arched wooden bridge. Over the following years he enlarged the water three times, planted weeping willows, agapanthus, bamboo, wisteria over the bridge, and the water lilies — hardy hybrids newly bred by Joseph Bory Latour-Marliac, in colours that no European water lily had had before. Monet’s water garden was, in effect, a piece of contemporary horticultural technology.

The Japanese Footbridge, 1899. The bridge, the pond and the lilies were all built and planted to be painted.

The painting problem he had set himself there was extraordinary. The surface of the pond is simultaneously a mirror (sky, clouds, the trees on the far bank), a window (the stems and shadows below), and an object (the lily pads lying flat on it). Three spatial systems in one plane, with no horizon to anchor them. The late water-lily canvases dispense with the bank entirely: there is no ground, no edge, no up. It is the closest a nineteenth-century painter came to abstraction while still, stubbornly, painting exactly what was in front of him.

Water Lilies, 1906. No bank, no horizon, no sky except the one reflected in the water.

Losing the light

From about 1905 Monet’s colour began to shift. He did not know why until 1912, when he was diagnosed with cataracts in both eyes. The lens of the eye yellows and clouds; blues and violets go first, and everything acquires a brown-red cast. He knew his canvases were changing and could not fully see how. He destroyed a number of them. He wrote that he was no longer capable of doing anything beautiful, and that he was ruining his pictures.

In 1923, aged eighty-two, he agreed to surgery on his right eye — three operations, the removal of the lens, months of dark rooms and misery, and a long, badly tolerated adjustment to the tinted spectacles that replaced it. Afterwards his colour vision was strange in a different way: an eye without a lens transmits near-ultraviolet light that a normal eye blocks, and there is reasonable evidence that Monet saw, and painted, blues and violets in places most people see white. Some of the last bridge paintings are a violent red-orange; others are drowned in blue. Both are, in their way, documentary.

The last room

On 12 November 1918, the day after the armistice, Monet wrote to his old friend Georges Clemenceau offering the state two decorative panels as a monument to peace. The offer grew into the Grandes Décorations: twenty-two enormous curved canvases, up to two metres high and six metres long, to be installed in two oval rooms so that the viewer stands inside an unbroken horizon of water, lilies and reflected sky.

He worked on them in a purpose-built studio at Giverny for the last eight years of his life, through the cataracts, the surgery, the death of his second wife Alice and of his son Jean, endlessly revising, repeatedly threatening to withdraw the gift. Clemenceau, by then out of office, bullied and coaxed him to the end. Monet refused to allow the panels to be shown while he lived.

He died at Giverny on 5 December 1926, aged eighty-six. The rooms at the Orangerie opened five months later, in May 1927, and were then largely ignored for thirty years — too decorative, too old-fashioned, a relic of a movement that had been overtaken twice. It took the American abstract painters of the 1950s, looking for ancestors who worked at wall scale in pure colour, to notice that the old man in the garden had got there first.
